summary: Earthrise is a free, browser-based tool for choosing where and when to land on the Moon’s south pole. There are three ways in: pick one of 34 known sites on a map (NASA’s nine Artemis III candidate regions, past and planned landers, high points and crater floors), pick any point of your own, or compare up to four landings side by side. For each landing, Earthrise answers in one line how long a solar-powered lander keeps power and how much of that time it can radio Earth directly — “Landing at de Gerlache Rim 2 on 1 January 2027: power for 3 days 4 hours, then night.” It then shows why, one step at a time: the Sun and Earth against the real hills hour by hour (NASA LRO LOLA elevation, JPL DE440 positions), the battery’s charge, the shadows on the ground, and a first-person view of the site under the real sky. It suggests a better landing day or a better place nearby, plans a landing from a typed or spoken mission description, and answers plain questions through Luna, a voice assistant that drives the app. Every number is computed in the browser from NASA data, and an Accuracy page shows how the results compare with JPL Horizons, NASA’s illumination maps and pictures from orbit, including the one check that misses its own mark.
details:
The problem

Landing at the lunar south pole turns on two questions:

  • When is the Sun above the local hills, so a solar lander has power?
  • When can the lander see Earth, so it can radio home?

The answers depend on terrain kilometres away, change hour by hour, and differ between sites a few kilometres apart. The tools that answer them exactly (SPICE, GIS stacks, illumination maps) take expertise and time to set up. Comparing two sites on two dates means running them again each time.

What Earthrise does

  • Three clear ways in. Pick a known site on the map, pick your own site (any point south of 60° S, worked out in the browser), or compare sites.
    • When a site is chosen, the page builds one part at a time, each with a "Next" button: where the site is, then the answer, then hour by hour, then the year, then the checks.
    • "Hour by hour" holds a chart of the Sun's and Earth's heights against the hills, the battery's charge, the radio windows, and the ground at that hour (a shadow map, the same light in 3D, and the horizon all round). A player plays the period.
    • "The year" colours every landing day of the next 12 months by power and radio contact.
    • Up to four landings: the same place on a later date, a place nearby, or any place and date.
    • Each landing has its own colour, a big number for time with power, and hour-by-hour strips of sunlight, Earth in view and radio contact.
    • Bars compare the key figures, the best values are marked, and one line says which landing works best and why.
  • Plan a landing from a mission description. Type or say what the mission needs, for example "at least five days of power, Earth in view when we land, a 300 W load and a 3 kWh battery, landing between March and June 2027". The planner reads it back as fields, tries every site and landing hour, and ranks them with their reasons.
  • Stand at the site. A first-person 3D view of the site under the real sky: NASA terrain to 125 km, the Sun at its true size, Earth and 8,404 real stars. The lander touches down, and the month can play by.
    • Every time carries a margin (for example ±8 h).
    • Explore shows how the answer changes across 32 versions of the ground at each polar site. These come from a statistical terrain-error model fitted to the differences between two generations of NASA's south-pole elevation maps.
    • Modelled cold traps from LRO Diviner are shown as conditions where ice could last, never as ice found.
  • Also: a one-page printable brief, share links, and a laptop mode that runs fully offline.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions come from an hourly table for 2024–2036, built with NASA/JPL SPICE from the DE440 ephemeris, and interpolated in the browser.
  • The hills on each site's horizon are traced in 720 directions through nested LRO LOLA elevation grids (20 m near the site, 80 m to 100 km, 240 m to 220 km), with the Moon's curvature.
  • Power = panel efficiency × area × solar constant × visible fraction of the Sun's disc × panel angle. The battery charges and discharges hour by hour.
  • Shadow maps sweep the elevation grids along the Sun's direction. The 3D view is lit with the same result.
  • A Python pipeline is the reference implementation. The TypeScript engine in the browser is pinned to it by test fixtures.

Validation (shown on the Accuracy page)

Three of the four checks meet their criteria. Past missions are context, not a check.

Evidence

Result

Sun and Earth directions vs JPL Horizons

300 comparisons; worst 0.00003° (target 0.01°). Live re-check button.

Sunlight vs NASA's LOLA illumination maps

Typical gap 0.9 percentage points at 15 sites.

Shadows vs 20 LRO camera pictures

92 % of the ground agrees in the typical picture (49 % with the Sun turned a quarter round). Misses its own mark: 17 of 20 pass. The 3 that miss had the Sun 1.1° up or less.

Power and battery sums

Agree with worked answers.

Context: Blue Ghost Mission 1

Its reported end came 2.4 h after the sunset Earthrise predicts.

Automated tests: 2,425 app tests and 257 pipeline tests pass. Browser journeys cover the main paths.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Mission planners: compare sites and dates in seconds, see the trade-offs between power, sunlight and radio contact, and hand a one-page brief to an engineering team.
    • The figures count electrical energy only, not thermal survival through the night.
    • Earth in view is geometric visibility, not a scheduled antenna pass.
    • Earthrise does not replace mission analysis.

Tools, languages and services

  • App: TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js (react-three-fiber), Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Web Workers.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, rasterio and spiceypy (NAIF SPICE).
  • Testing: Vitest and Playwright.
  • Hosting: Vercel, with Cloudflare R2 for the data files.
  • AI APIs: OpenRouter and Google Gemini.
